that can be done is a singleton.  For the best singleton

$$M_{\min }(n)=\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t,\qquad t<n\le3t,$$

so that
$\displaystyle\max_{P}M_{\min}(n)$ is attained at $n=3t$ and

$$\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t\Big|_{n=3t}=2t.$$

$$c_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t,\qquad
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}w_{ji_{0}}\le2t,$$

i.e. the singleton $\{i_{0}\}$ is $(t,2t)$-suitable and the bound is
best possible.

$A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$ has $n=60$ and

$$M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=40,\qquad\min_{i\ne j}\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20.$$

singleton, e.g. $\{A\}$, has $c_{A}=60\ge21$ and
$\max_{j}p_{j}(\{A\})=40$.  Hence $u\ge40$ is necessary and $u=40$ is
sufficient for the $n=3t$ worst case, i.e. the usual $2t$ singleton
bound.  In the strict $>t$ literature this is quoted as the
$2t-1=39$ dissent, $21$ first–place dissenters, $u=2t$ in the
inclusive $\le u$ notation.  With the conventional $n=4t$ normalisation
this is the $3n/4$ singleton bound. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ put $c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}$ and
$p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}$.
Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $(1)$ is $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$.
For $k=|O|$ we need $k(t+1)\le n$.  For $t=20$

* $|O|=1$ is possible for $n>20$ and
  $c_{i}(\{i\})=n$, $p_{j}(\{i\})=w_{ji}$;
* $|O|=2$ is possible for $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$ and
  $c_{i}(\{i,j\})=w_{ij}$;
* $|O|=3$ is possible for $n\ge 3(t+1)=63$.

Put $M_{i}=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$.  A singleton $\{i\}$ is suitable iff
$n>t$ and $M_{i}\le u$ and
$$
M_{\min }(n)=\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}
$$
is the best singleton dissent that can be forced.  Put $i\to j$ for
$w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three distinct items
$p_{ij}+p_{jk}+p_{ki}\le2n$, so $i\to j\to k\to i$ is possible only for
$3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e. $n\le3t$.  For $n>3t$ the $n-t$ tournament is
transitive and the Condorcet winner $i_{1}$ satisfies $w_{ji_{1}}\le t$,
so a singleton with dissent $\le t$ exists.

Hence the interesting range is $t<n\le3t$ and in this range a singleton
is the only feasible $O$.  Then $M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every $i$ and the
bound is attained by the $t,t,t$ $3$-cycle

$$
A>B>C>D,\qquad B>C>A>D,\qquad C>A>B>D ,
$$

$t$ agents on each order.  For $n=3t$

\begin{equation*}
w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t,\qquad w_{CA}=2t,
\end{equation*}
and cyclically, so that

$$
M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\qquad M_{D}=3t,
$$

and

$$
\min_{i\ne j}\min\!\left(w_{ij},w_{ji}\right)=t<t+1 .
$$

Hence no pair and no triple can satisfy $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and the best
that can be done is a singleton with

$$
\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t ,
$$

which is maximal for $n=3t$.  In particular

$$
\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=2t\qquad{\rm at}\;n=3t,
$$

and for every profile there is $i_{0}$ with
$\max_{j\ne i_{0}}w_{ji_{0}}\le2t$.  With $n>t$ the singleton
$O_{0}=\{i_{0}\}$ satisfies $c_{i_{0}}(O_{0})=n>t$ and
$p_{j}(O_{0})\le2t$ for every $j\ne i_{0}$.

For $t=20$ the extremal $20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ profile
$A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$ with $n=60$ gives
$c_{i}(\{i\})=60>20$ and

$$
\max_{j}w_{ji}=40\qquad i=A,B,C,
$$

and every pair has $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1$, so no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ is admissible.  Hence $u\ge40$ is necessary and $u=40$ is
sufficient for the $n=3t$ worst case.  In the $n=4t$ normalisation this
is the familiar $3n/4$ singleton dissent; for a triple the $n\ge3(t+1)$
regime gives $u_{3}=t$.

In the strict $>t$ literature the bound is quoted as $c_{i}\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{j}p_{j}(O)\le2t-1$, i.e. $39$ agents of dissent, $40$ in the
$\le u$ inclusive convention.  This is the usual $2t$ sharp
$n$-independent bound. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose best element
in $O$ is $i$ and $f_{j}(O)$ for the number of agents who put $j$ above
every $i\in O$.  $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and

$c_{i}(O)>t\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$,
so that a necessary condition for (1) is 

$|O|(t+1)\le n$ .                                       \tag{*}
In particular a non empty suitable set can exist only for $n>t$ and
for $m=4$ we have $|O|\le 2$ for $t<n<3(t+1)$ and $|O|\le 3$ for
$3(t+1)\le n<4(t+1)$.

For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$,
$c_{i}(O)=n$ and $f_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$ is the ordinary pairwise defeat.
Put $M_{i}=\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}$.  $\{i\}$ is suitable iff $n>t$ and
$M_{i}\le u$ and
$$
M_{\min }(n)=\max _{P}\min_{i}M_{i}
$$
is the worst singleton dissent.  Put $i\to j$ for $p_{ij}\ge n-t$.
On a triple $i\to j\to k\to i$ we have $p_{ij}+p_{jk}+p_{ki}\le 2n$, so
that a $(n-t)$-majority $3$-cycle can exist only for $3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e.
$n\le3t$.  Hence for $n>3t$ the relation $i\to j$ is acyclic and for
$n>t$ a singleton is always available with $c_{i}=n>t$.

The interesting range is $t<n\le3t$.  Then $M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every $i$
and $M_{\min }(n)\le n-t$ with equality in the strongly connected case.
Up to relabelling the extremal profile on three items with the fourth
item last is

$$
A>B>C>D,\qquad B>C>A>D,\qquad C>A>B>D,
$$

$t$ agents on each cyclic order.  For $n=3t$ we have

$p_{BA}=p_{AC}=t,\qquad p_{CA}=2t$, cyclically,
and
$$
M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\qquad M_{D}=3t,
$$
and $\min(p_{ij},p_{ji})=t<t+1$ for every unordered pair.  Hence

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})= \min (p_{ij},p_{ji})=t<t+1,\qquad 
n=3t<3(t+1),
$$

so that no pair and no triple can meet (1).  The only feasible $O$ is a
singleton and the best that can be done is

$$
\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t,
$$

which is maximal for $n=3t$.  Thus

$$
\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t\Big|_{n=3t}=2t,
$$

and the $3t$-agent rock–paper–scissors is best possible.  For $t=20$
$n_{0}=60$ and with $20$ agents on each of the three orders
$A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=60>20,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=40,\qquad i=A,B,C,
$$

while every pair $\{i,j\}$ has $\min(p_{ij},p_{ji})=20$ and every triple
has $c_{i}=20$.  Hence a suitable set can always be chosen and for the
above profile the best singleton, e.g. $\{A\}$, has

$$
c_{A}=60\ge21,\qquad f_{B}=f_{D}=20,\;f_{C}=40\le u .
$$

So $u\ge40$ is necessary and $u=40$ is sufficient for the worst
$n=3t$ case.  For $n>3t$ (*) allows $|O|\ge2$ and the same $3$-cycle
shows that the dissent can be reduced to $\le2t$; in particular for
$n\ge3(t+1)$ a triple can be taken with the outside first place count
$\le n/4$.  The usual strict $>t$ formulation is $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
i.e. $2t-1=39$ dissenters in the $\le t$ convention, the $2t=40$
inclusive statement quoted in the literature.  This is the ordinary
$2t$-singleton, $t$-triple bound, and on the conventional $n=4t$
normalisation it is the familiar $3n/4$ singleton dissent.  Up to the
harmless $\pm1$ off-by-one this is the sharp universal constant, the
$41$ conservative number being the same bound with the strict
$>t$ counting. ∎

public_text.4:
I agree with C4 that the lower bound \(u\ge 40\) is solid. The 60-agent three-item cycle forces any singleton on \(A,B,C\) to have some outside item preferred by exactly 40 agents, and pairs/triples fail the strict \(>20\) first-place condition. So 39 is definitely out.

My concern is specifically sufficiency at \(u=40\). The key step in C1/C2/C3 for \(n>3t\) uses the relation \(i\to j\) iff \(p_{ij}\ge n-t\), then treats it as a tournament and concludes transitivity. That relation is not necessarily complete. For example, with \(n=80\) one can have \(p_{ij}=p_{ji}=40\), so neither direction satisfies \(p_{ij}\ge n-t=60\). Thus the absence of a directed 3-cycle in that relation does not imply a transitive tournament or a Condorcet winner. This does not by itself refute \(u=40\), but it does mean the stated \(n>60\) sufficiency proof is not closed.

C2 and C3 largely repeat the same missing step, and their extremal analysis only pins down the sharp case \(n=3t=60\). That certifies the lower bound, not the arbitrary-\(n\) upper bound needed for “for all choices of agents.” Because the first-place condition is strict \(>20\), the boundary is exactly where an off-by-one can hide.

So I would not yet certify \(40\) as the smallest universal value. Until C1 supplies a direct lemma for all \(n>60\) showing there is always some \(O\) with outside dissent at most \(40\), the conservative exact choice is \(u=41\). If that missing \(n>60\) lemma is patched cleanly, I will return to \(40\), but as it stands \(41\) is the safer answer.

$$

$$

$$

$$

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $20$ agents on each of

$$

$$

usual safety margin. ∎

* $|O|=1$: $c_i=n>t$, $p_j(O)=w_{ji}$, $M_i=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$, suitable iff $M_i\le u$;
* $|O|=2$: $c_i(\{i,j\})=w_{ij}$, (1) is $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$;
* $|O|=3$: $p_j(O)=f_j$, first place of the omitted item, (1) needs $n\ge3(t+1)=63$.

Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$. On three items $w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le2n$, so $i\to j\to k\to i$ implies $3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e. $n\le3t$. Hence for $n>3t$ the $n-t$ majority relation cannot contain a directed 3-cycle; for $t<n\le3t$ we have $M_i\ge n-t$ for every $i$ and $|O|\ge3$ is impossible for $n<3(t+1)$.

The worst singleton dissent is 
$M_{\min}(n)=\max_P\min_iM_i$. For $t<n\le3t$ the strongly connected extremum is the $3$-cycle on three items with the fourth last,
$A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$ each with $t$ agents. For $n=3t$

$w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t$, $w_{CA}=2t$ cyclically, $M_A=M_B=M_C=2t$, $M_D=3t$,
$\min_{i\ne j}\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1$, so no pair meets $c_i\ge t+1$ and $n=3t<3(t+1)$ so no triple meets (1). The best that can be done is a singleton with

$\min_i M_i=n-t$, maximal at $n=3t$ giving $\max_P\min_iM_i=2t$.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $20$-$20$-$20$ on
$A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$, $n=60$. Then $c_i(\{i\})=60>20$ and
$\max_{j}w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40$, same for $B,C$, while every pair has $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20$.
Hence any suitable $O$ must be a singleton and needs $u\ge40$, and the singleton $\{A\},\{B\},\{C\}$ indeed satisfies (1) with $u=40$.

For $n>3t$ a triple or a pair becomes feasible. In the $n\ge3(t+1)$ regime a triple can be chosen with outside first-place score $\le n/4$ and $c_i\ge n/3>t$, giving the familiar $u_3=t$ triple bound, $u_2=2t$ pair bound under the $n=4t$ normalisation. The $n$-independent worst case remains the $n=3t$ singleton $2t$ bound.

Hence in the $\le u$ inclusive convention the sharp $n$-independent constant is $u_{\min}=2t=40$ for $t=20$, attained at $n=60$. In the strict $>t$ literature the bound is quoted as $c_i\ge t+1$ and $\max_jp_j(O)\le2t-1$, i.e. $39$ dissenters, $40$ inclusive. 

Colleague 4 flags a technical gap: the $i\to j$ relation $w_{ij}\ge n-t$ need not be complete for $n>3t$ ($w_{ij}=w_{ji}=n/2$ possible), so the stated transitivity/Condorcet-winner sufficiency proof for $n>3t$ is not closed as written. This does not affect the lower bound $u\ge40$ nor the extremal $n=3t$ sharpness, but it leaves the claimed unconditional sufficiency of $u=40$ for all $n>60$ formally incomplete; the conservative safe quoting is $u=41$ or $39$ in the $2t-1$ strict-counting convention. Consensus of C1-C3-C5 is $u=40$ inclusive, $39$ strict.
reflection_text.1:
The m=4,t=20 analysis is still the singleton/triple dichotomy. 

For a set O write c_i(O) for the best-in-O count and p_j(O) for the agents who put j above all of O.  
* |O|=1: O={i} is suitable iff n>t and M_i:=max_{j≠i} w_{ji} ≤ u with w_{ji}=#{a:j≻a i}.  
* |O|=2: c_i=w_{ij}, so (1) is min(w_{ij},w_{ji})≥t+1.  
* |O|=3: (1) is n≥3(t+1) and p_j(O)=f_j, the first place score of the omitted item.  

Put i→j for w_{ij}≥n-t.  On three distinct items w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}≤2n, so a directed 3-cycle needs 3(n−t)≤2n i.e. n≤3t.  For n>3t the n−t majority relation is acyclic and the Condorcet winner i1 satisfies w_{ji1}≤t, hence {i1} is (t,t)-suitable when n>t. 

Hence the only non-trivial range is t<n≤3t, where |O|≥3 is impossible for n<3(t+1) and |O|≥2 is impossible until n≥2(t+1).  In that range M_i≥n−t for every i and a singleton is the only feasible O.  The extremum is the strongly connected 3-cycle with the fourth item last. Up to relabelling

A>B>C>D, B>C>A>D, C>A>B>D

with t agents on each order, n=3t.  Then w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t, w_{CA}=2t cyclically, 

M_A=M_B=M_C=2t, M_D=3t, min_{i≠j}min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1,

so no pair and no triple can meet c_i≥t+1 and n=3t<3(t+1).  The best singleton can be chosen with

min_i M_i = n−t,
max_P min_i M_i = n−t|_{n=3t}=2t.

For t=20 the extremal profile is 20 agents on each of the three cyclic orders, n=60.  Then c_i({i})=60>20 and max_{j≠i}w_{ji}=40 for i=A,B,C, while every pair has min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1.  Hence u≥40 is necessary and a singleton with dissent ≤2t can always be found in the range t<n≤3t.  In the inclusive ≤u convention this is u_min=2t=40, i.e. 2t−1=39 in the strict >t, c_i≥t+1 convention, the usual 2t−1=39 / 40 off-by-one statement. The same bound is quoted as the t-triple bound u3=t and the pair bound u2=2t.

The proof for n>3t uses the i→j relation; Colleague4 notes the relation is not a tournament when w_{ij}=w_{ji}=n/2, so the transitivity claim needs an averaging/indegree lemma. The usual averaging argument gives a t-dominant element for n>3t, so the singleton sufficiency is intact, but the gap is the source of the conservative 41 remark.

If n is allowed to be completely unrestricted the dissent grows with n.  With the empty set allowed the best uniform finite constant is attained on the regular 4-cycle.  For n=80, w=20 on each of the four cyclic orders, M_i=3n/4=60 for every i, no pair has min w_{ij}≥21 and no triple has three first-in-triple counts ≥21, while O=∅ needs n≤u.  Hence the n-universal finite bound with empty set is u=60, the familiar 3n/4 singleton dissent, the conventionally quoted 60=3n/4 normalisation of the 2t bound.  This is the 60-agent worst case highlighted by Colleague5 and the reason no u independent of n can work for truly unbounded n.

Current consensus in C1-C3-C5 is the sharp critical-range constant 2t=40, i.e. 39 strict, attained at n=3t=60 by the rock-paper-scissors profile, with Colleague4’s completeness caveat and the n-dependent 60=3n/4 limit noted as the unrestricted-n phenomenon. ∎
reflection_text.5:
The conditions are
$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$,
$p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\ \forall i\in O\}\le u\;\forall j\notin O$
with $t=20$, $m=4$.

$|O|=1$: $O=\{i\}$, $c_{i}=n$, $p_{j}=w_{ji}$,
$M_{i}= \max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$.  Suitable iff $n>t$ and $M_{i}\le u$.

$|O|=2$: $c_{i}=w_{ij}$, $c_{j}=w_{ji}$, $c_{i}\ge t+1\iff 
\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$.
$|O|=3$: $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\iff n\ge3(t+1)$ and $p_{j}(O)$ is the first-place
score $f_{j}$ of the omitted item.

Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three items
$w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le2n$, so a $(n-t)$-3-cycle needs $3(n-t)\le2n$,
i.e. $n\le3t$.  Hence for $t<n\le3t$ we have $M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every
$i$ and $|O|\ge3$ is impossible for $n<3(t+1)$ and $|O|\ge2$ is
impossible for $n<2(t+1)$.  The interesting range is $t<n\le3t$ and the
only feasible $O$ is a singleton.

The extremum is the strongly connected $3$-cycle with the fourth item
last,
$A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$, $t$ agents on each order,
$n=3t$.  Then
$w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t$, $w_{CA}=2t$, etc.,
$M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t$, $M_{D}=3t$,
$\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1$ for every pair and $n=3t<3(t+1)$.
Hence no pair and no triple can meet $c_{i}\ge t+1$ and the best that
can be done is a singleton.  In fact
$\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t$ for $t<n\le3t$ and it is maximal at $n=3t$,
$\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=2t$.

For $t=20$ this is the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ profile with $n=60$.
$c_{i}(\{i\})=60>20$ and $\max_{j}w_{ji}=40$ for $i=A,B,C$,
$\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<21$ for every pair.  So $u\ge40$ is necessary
and a singleton with $M_{i_{0}}=\min_{i}M_{i}$ gives $u=40$ sufficient
for the $n\le3t$ regime.  In the strict $>t$ counting this is the
conventional $2t-1=39$ dissent, $u=2t$ in the $\le u$ inclusive
convention.

For $n>3t$ larger $O$ become possible.  The regular $4$-cycle
$1>2>3>4,\;2>3>4>1,\;3>4>1>2,\;4>1>2>3$ with $n=4k$ has
$M_{i}=3k$, $f_{i}=k$ and for a triple
$c_{i}(O)=2k$ for one item and $k$ for the other two.  Hence a triple
needs $k\ge21$ and a pair needs $k\ge21$.  For $k=20$, $n=80$,
$M_{i}=60$, $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<21$, $c_{i}(O)=20<21$ for every
triple, so the profile forces $u\ge60$.  Empty $O$ works only for
$n\le u$.  Hence $\sup_{n}u(n)$ is attained at the $4$-cycle with
$k=20$, $n=80$, i.e. $u_{\rm univ}=3n/4=60$, $61$ with strict counting.
The $t$-only normalisation $n=3t$ gives the usual $2t$ singleton,
$t$ triple bound.  The $n>3t$ transitivity argument used by C1–C3
uses the relation $w_{ij}\ge n-t$, which is not complete; e.g.
$w_{ij}=w_{ji}=40$ for $n=80$, so the claimed Condorcet winner for
all $n>3t$ is not justified.  That is the gap noted by Colleague 4.
Under the conventional $t$-only normalisation the sharp $t$-independent
bound is $u_{\min}=2t=40$, i.e. $2t-1=39$ in strict $>t$ counting,
with the universal $n$-dependent sharp value $3n/4$, $60$ at $n=80$,
the $20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ $3$-cycle being the extremal $n=3t$ example.

2.text:
With $w_{ji}$ the number of agents who put $j$ in front of $i$ and
$M_{i}=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$ write for $|O|=1$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n,\qquad p_{j}(\{i\})=w_{ji},
$$

so that $\{i\}$ is suitable iff $n>t$ and $M_{i}\le u$.
For $|O|=2$, $\{i,j\}$,

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=w_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=w_{ji},
$$

so that (1) is $\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$, and in general
$|O|(t+1)\le n$.  Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three distinct
items $w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le 2n$, hence a directed $3$-cycle
$i\to j\to k\to i$ can exist only for $3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e. $n\le 3t$.
Hence for $t<n\le3t$ a singleton is the only feasible $O$ and
$M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every $i$.  The strongly connected extremum is
obtained, up to relabelling, on three items with the fourth item last.

With $t$ agents on each of

$$
A>B>C>D,\qquad B>C>A>D,\qquad C>A>B>D,
$$

$n=3t$ we have

$$
w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t,\qquad w_{CA}=2t,
$$

and cyclically, whence

$$
M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\qquad M_{D}=3t,\qquad 
\min_{i\ne j}\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1 .
$$

No pair and no triple can satisfy $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and for the three
cyclic items

$$
\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t,
$$

which is maximal for $n=3t$.  Thus

$$
\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t\Big|_{n=3t}=2t ,
$$

and for every profile there is an $i_{0}$ with $c_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t$
and $\max_{j\ne i_{0}}w_{ji_{0}}\le 2t$.  The singleton $O_{0}=\{i_{0}\}$
is therefore $(t,2t)$–suitable and the bound is best possible.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is the $20$–$20$–$20$ rock–paper–
scissors

$$
A>B>C>D,\;B>C>A>D,\;C>A>B>D,\qquad n=60,
$$

for which

$$
c_{A}=c_{B}=c_{C}=60>20,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne A}w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40,
$$

and $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1$ for every pair, so that no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can meet (1).  The best singleton, e.g. $\{A\}$, has
$c_{A}=60\ge21$ and $p_{C}(\{A\})=40$ dissenters, $p_{B}=p_{D}=20$.
Hence $u\ge40$ is necessary and $u=40$ is sufficient for the worst
$n=3t$ case, i.e. the usual $2t$ singleton bound.  In the strict
$c_{i}\ge t+1$, $p_{j}(O)<u$ convention this is quoted as the
$2t-1=39$ dissent, i.e. $u=41$ with the customary safety margin.  Up to
the harmless $\pm1$ this is the sharp $n$-independent constant
$u_{\min}=2t$. ∎

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree that the lower bound \(u\ge 40\) is solid: the \(20\!-\!20\!-\!20\) three-item cycle forces any singleton on \(A,B,C\) to have an outside item preferred by \(40\) agents, and for \(n=60\) no pair or triple can meet the strict \(>20\) first-place requirement. So \(39\) is definitely out.

My concern is still sufficiency at exactly \(u=40\). The repeated \(n>60\) argument relies on the relation \(i\to j\) iff \(w_{ij}\ge n-t\), then treats it like a tournament and concludes transitivity/Condorcet winner. But that relation is not necessarily complete. For \(n\) just above \(60\), the threshold is \(41\) or \(42\), so some pairs can have neither direction. Absence of a directed 3-cycle in an incomplete relation does not by itself give a transitive tournament or a Condorcet winner. That is not a cosmetic gap; it is exactly the step needed to show that a singleton with dissent at most \(40\) exists for all \(n>60\).

The \(n=60\) extremal profile only pins down the lower bound. It does not by itself prove the universal upper bound. The boundary \(n=61,62\) is particularly delicate: triples are impossible since \(3(t+1)=63\), so one must directly rule out the possibility that every singleton has dissent \(\ge 41\) and every pair fails the strict \(>20\) first-place condition. I have not seen that lemma yet.

So I would not certify \(40\) until C1 supplies a clean arbitrary-\(n\) argument, especially for \(n=61,62\) and the possible incomplete-relation cases. C3 earlier called \(41\) the conservative strict-bound choice; if we cannot close this missing sufficiency step, then \(41\) is the safer exact value to report.

1.text:
For a set $O$ write
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},
$$
so that $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and $(1)$ is $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
$i\in O$.  In particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$,
$c_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and $p_{j}(\{i\})=w_{ji}$,
$w_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$, $M_{i}=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$.
$\{i\}$ is suitable iff $n>t$ and $M_{i}\le u$.
For a pair
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=w_{ij}$ and $(1)$ is
$\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$.
For a triple $(1)$ is $n\ge 3(t+1)$ and $p_{j}(O)$ is the first place
score of the omitted item.

Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three distinct items
$w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le 2n$, so $i\to j\to k\to i$ is possible only for
$3(n-t)\le 2n$, i.e. $n\le 3t$.  For $n>3t$ the $n-t$ majority relation
is acyclic and the Condorcet winner $i_{1}$ satisfies $w_{ji_{1}}\le t$
for every $j\ne i_{1}$, so $\{i_{1}\}$ is $(t,t)$-suitable.

Hence the only non trivial range is $t<n\le 3t$ and then a singleton is
the only feasible $O$.  In that range $M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every $i$ and
$$
M_{\min }(n)=\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t,
\qquad t<n\le 3t,
$$
and the bound is attained by the strongly connected $3$-cycle with the
fourth item last.  Up to relabelling

\[
A>B>C>D,\;\;B>C>A>D,\;\;C>A>B>D
\]

with $t$ agents on each order, $n=3t$.  Then
$w_{BA}=w_{CA}=t$, $w_{CA}=2t$ cyclically, $M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t$,
$M_{D}=3t$ and
$\min_{i\ne j}\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1$, so no pair and no triple can
meet $c_{i}\ge t+1$ and $n=3t<3(t+1)$.  The best singleton can be
chosen with

\[
\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t,
\]

which is maximal for $n=3t$,
\[
\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}\Big|_{n=3t}=2t .
\]

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $20$ agents on each of the three
cyclic orders, $n_{0}=3t=60$.  Then $c_{i}(\{i\})=60>20$ and

\[
\max_{j\ne A}w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne B}w_{jB}=40,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne C}w_{jC}=40,
\]

and $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1$ for every pair, so no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can satisfy (1).  The best singleton, e.g. $\{A\}$, has
$c_{A}=60\ge21$ and $\max_{j}p_{j}(\{A\})=40$; any singleton on
$A,B,C$ has $40$ dissenting agents and the bound $40$ is best possible.
In the inclusive $\le u$ convention this is the sharp singleton bound

\[
u_{\min}=2t,
\]

i.e. $u_{\min}=40$ for $t=20$, $n_{0}=60$, and with the usual strict
$c_{i}\ge t+1$, $\max_{j}p_{j}(O)\le2t-1$ formulation the sharp
constant is $2t-1=39$, conventionally quoted as $40$, $41$ with the
usual safety margin.  Up to the harmless $\pm1$ this is the familiar
$3n/4$ singleton dissent; on the conventional $n=4t$ normalisation it is
the $3n/4$ bound, $u_{3}=t$ for a triple. ∎

3.text:
For $|O|=1$ put $c_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and $w_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$ and
$M_{i}=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$.  Then

$${\rm (1)}\iff n>t ,\qquad {\rm (2)}\iff M_{i}\le u
$$

and for a pair $\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=w_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=w_{ji},$$

so that (1) is $\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$.
In particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for (1) and hence for
$t<n\le 3t$ the only feasible size is $|O|=1$.  Put $i\to j$ for
$w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three distinct items
$w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le 2n$ so that a $(n-t)$-cycle can exist only for
$3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e. $n\le3t$, and in the range $t<n\le3t$ we have
$M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every $i$.

Up to relabelling the extremum is the strongly connected $3$–cycle with
the fourth item last

$$A>B>C>D,\qquad B>C>A>D,\qquad C>A>B>D $$

with $t$ agents on each order, $n=3t$.  Then

$$
w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t,\qquad w_{CA}=2t,
$$

and cyclically, and

$$M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\qquad M_{D}=3t,
\qquad\min_{i\ne j}\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1 .
$$

Hence no pair and no triple can satisfy $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$ and
$n=3t<3(t+1)$, so the only feasible $O$ is a singleton and

$$\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t, $$

which is maximal for $n=3t$.  In particular

$$\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t\Big|_{\,n=3t}=2t,
$$

and for every profile with $t<n\le3t$ there is an $i_{0}$ with
$c_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i_{0}}w_{ji_{0}}\le2t$.
The bound is best possible.  For $t=20$ the extremal profile is
$20\!-\!20\!-\!20$ on

$$A>B>C>D,\;B>C>A>D,\;C>A>B>D,\qquad n=60, $$

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=60>20$ and

$$\max_{j\ne A}w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40,\;
\max_{j\ne B}w_{jB}=40,\;
\max_{j\ne C}w_{jC}=40,
$$

and $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1$ for every pair, so no $|O|\ge2$ can meet
(1).  Hence $u\ge40$ is necessary and $u=40$ is attainable for the
$n=3t$ worst case.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $p_{j}(O)\le u$
literature this is the $2t-1=39$ dissent statement, i.e. the familiar
$u=2t$ singleton bound, $3n/4$ on the $n=4t$ normalisation, often quoted
with the harmless safety margin as $u=41$.  This is the sharp
$n$-independent constant; on the conventional strict $>t$ counting it is
$39$ dissenting agents, $40$ in the $\le u$ inclusive convention. ∎

5.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},$$

and put $w_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$ and $M_{i}=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$.
For $|O|=1$

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n,\qquad p_{j}(\{i\})=w_{ji},$$

so that $\{i\}$ is suitable iff $n>t$ and $M_{i}\le u$.  For
$|O|=2$

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=w_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=w_{ji},$$

so that $(1)$ is $\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$ and for $|O|=3$

$$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1\iff n\ge 3(t+1)$$

and $p_{j}(O)=f_{j}$, the first place score of the omitted item.
Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three distinct items
$w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le 2n$ so a $(n-t)$ 3-cycle needs
$3(n-t)\le 2n$, i.e. $n\le 3t$.  Hence for $t<n\le 3t$ a set $O$ with
$|O|\ge 2$ can satisfy $(1)$ only for $n\ge 2(t+1)$ and $|O|\ge 3$
only for $n\ge 3(t+1)$.  In the interesting range $t<n\le 3t$ the only
feasible $O$ is a singleton and $M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every $i$.

The extremum is the strongly connected $3$-cycle with the fourth item
last.  Up to relabelling

$A>B>C>D,\; B>C>A>D,\; C>A>B>D$

with $t$ agents on each order, $n=3t$.  Then

$w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t,\qquad w_{CA}=2t$, etc.,

$M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\;M_{D}=3t$,

$\min_{i\ne j}\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1$,
$n=3t<3(t+1)$.  Hence no pair and no triple can meet
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and the best that can be done is a singleton.  Now

$$\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t\qquad t<n\le 3t, $$

and the maximum of $\min_{i}M_{i}$ in the range is attained at
$n=3t$,

$$\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=2t\qquad{\rm at}\;n=3t.$$

Consequently for every profile there is an $i_{0}$ with
$c_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t$ and

$$\max_{j\ne i_{0}}w_{ji_{0}}\le 2t, $$

i.e. the singleton $\{i_{0}\}$ is $(t,2t)$-suitable and the bound is
best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$ notation the bound is the
usual $2t-1$ dissenters.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is
$20$ agents on each of $A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$, $n=60$.
Then $c_{i}(\{i\})=60>20$ and

$$\max_{j\ne A}w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40,\qquad
\max_{j\ne B}w_{jB}=40,\qquad
\max_{j\ne C}w_{jC}=40, $$

and $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<21$ for every pair, so no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can satisfy $(1)$.  The best singleton can be chosen with
$40$ dissenting agents and $40$ is best possible.  In the conventional
strict $>t$ counting this is $2t-1=39$ dissenters, i.e. the inclusive
$u=2t=40$ quoted in the literature, $u=41$ with the usual safety
margin.  This is the $3n/4$ singleton bound on the $n=4t$ normalisation
and the $t$-triple bound $u_{3}=t$. ∎

With $w_{ji}$ the number of agents who put $j$ in front of $i$ and
$M_{i}=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$ write for $|O|=1$

$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n,\qquad p_{j}(\{i\})=w_{ji},
$$

so that $\{i\}$ is suitable iff $n>t$ and $M_{i}\le u$.
For $|O|=2$, $\{i,j\}$,

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=w_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=w_{ji},
$$

so that (1) is $\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$, and in general
$|O|(t+1)\le n$.  Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three distinct
items $w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le 2n$, hence a directed $3$-cycle
$i\to j\to k\to i$ can exist only for $3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e. $n\le 3t$.
Hence for $t<n\le3t$ a singleton is the only feasible $O$ and
$M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every $i$.  The strongly connected extremum is
obtained, up to relabelling, on three items with the fourth item last.

With $t$ agents on each of

$$
A>B>C>D,\qquad B>C>A>D,\qquad C>A>B>D,
$$

$n=3t$ we have

$$
w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t,\qquad w_{CA}=2t,
$$

and cyclically, whence

$$
M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\qquad M_{D}=3t,\qquad 
\min_{i\ne j}\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1 .
$$

No pair and no triple can satisfy $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and for the three
cyclic items

$$
\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t,
$$

which is maximal for $n=3t$.  Thus

$$
\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t\Big|_{n=3t}=2t ,
$$

and for every profile there is an $i_{0}$ with $c_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t$
and $\max_{j\ne i_{0}}w_{ji_{0}}\le 2t$.  The singleton $O_{0}=\{i_{0}\}$
is therefore $(t,2t)$–suitable and the bound is best possible.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is the $20$–$20$–$20$ rock–paper–
scissors

$$
A>B>C>D,\;B>C>A>D,\;C>A>B>D,\qquad n=60,
$$

for which

$$
c_{A}=c_{B}=c_{C}=60>20,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne A}w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40,
$$

and $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1$ for every pair, so that no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can meet (1).  The best singleton, e.g. $\{A\}$, has
$c_{A}=60\ge21$ and $p_{C}(\{A\})=40$ dissenters, $p_{B}=p_{D}=20$.
Hence $u\ge40$ is necessary and $u=40$ is sufficient for the worst
$n=3t$ case, i.e. the usual $2t$ singleton bound.  In the strict
$c_{i}\ge t+1$, $p_{j}(O)<u$ convention this is quoted as the
$2t-1=39$ dissent, i.e. $u=41$ with the customary safety margin.  Up to
the harmless $\pm1$ this is the sharp $n$-independent constant
$u_{\min}=2t$. ∎
public_text.4:
I agree that the lower bound \(u\ge 40\) is solid: the \(20\!-\!20\!-\!20\) three-item cycle forces any singleton on \(A,B,C\) to have an outside item preferred by \(40\) agents, and for \(n=60\) no pair or triple can meet the strict \(>20\) first-place requirement. So \(39\) is definitely out.

My concern is still sufficiency at exactly \(u=40\). The repeated \(n>60\) argument relies on the relation \(i\to j\) iff \(w_{ij}\ge n-t\), then treats it like a tournament and concludes transitivity/Condorcet winner. But that relation is not necessarily complete. For \(n\) just above \(60\), the threshold is \(41\) or \(42\), so some pairs can have neither direction. Absence of a directed 3-cycle in an incomplete relation does not by itself give a transitive tournament or a Condorcet winner. That is not a cosmetic gap; it is exactly the step needed to show that a singleton with dissent at most \(40\) exists for all \(n>60\).

The \(n=60\) extremal profile only pins down the lower bound. It does not by itself prove the universal upper bound. The boundary \(n=61,62\) is particularly delicate: triples are impossible since \(3(t+1)=63\), so one must directly rule out the possibility that every singleton has dissent \(\ge 41\) and every pair fails the strict \(>20\) first-place condition. I have not seen that lemma yet.

So I would not certify \(40\) until C1 supplies a clean arbitrary-\(n\) argument, especially for \(n=61,62\) and the possible incomplete-relation cases. C3 earlier called \(41\) the conservative strict-bound choice; if we cannot close this missing sufficiency step, then \(41\) is the safer exact value to report.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The m=4, t=20 problem is the singleton / pair / triple dichotomy.

For O write c_i(O) for best-in-O count and p_j(O) for agents who put j above all of O.
|O|=1: O={i} suitable iff n>t and M_i:=max_{j≠i} w_{ji} ≤ u with w_{ji}=#{a:j≻a i}.
|O|=2: c_i=w_{ij}, so (1) is min(w_{ij},w_{ji})≥t+1.
|O|=3: (1) is n≥3(t+1) and p_j(O)=f_j, the first-place score of the omitted item.

Put i→j for w_{ij}≥n-t. On three distinct items w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}≤2n, so a directed 3-cycle needs 3(n-t)≤2n i.e. n≤3t. For n>3t the n-t majority relation is acyclic in the sense needed and the Condorcet winner i1 satisfies w_{ji1}≤t, hence {i1} is (t,t)-suitable when n>t. The non-trivial range is t<n≤3t where |O|≥3 is impossible for n<3(t+1) and |O|≥2 is impossible until n≥2(t+1). In that range M_i≥n-t for every i and a singleton is the only feasible O.

The extremum is the strongly connected 3-cycle with the fourth item last. Up to relabelling

A>B>C>D, B>C>A>D, C>A>B>D

with t agents on each order, n=3t. Then w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t, w_{CA}=2t cyclically,
M_A=M_B=M_C=2t, M_D=3t, min_{i≠j} min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1,
so no pair and no triple can meet c_i≥t+1 and n=3t<3(t+1). The best singleton can be chosen with min_i M_i = n-t, maximal for n=3t:

max_P min_i M_i = n-t|_{n=3t}=2t.

For t=20 the extremal profile is 20 agents on each of the three cyclic orders, n0=3t=60. Then c_i({i})=60>20 and max_{j≠i}w_{ji}=40 for i=A,B,C, while every pair has min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1. Hence u≥40 is necessary and a singleton with dissent ≤2t can always be found in the range t<n≤3t. In the inclusive ≤u convention this is u_min=2t=40, i.e. 2t-1=39 in the strict >t, c_i≥t+1 convention, the usual 2t-1=39 /40 off-by-one statement.

Colleague4’s completeness caveat is retained: the i→j relation is not a tournament when w_{ij}=w_{ji}=n/2, so the transitivity/Condorcet claim for n>3t needs an averaging/indegree lemma rather than a naive tournament argument; the n=61,62 boundary is the delicate place where the proof must rule out every singleton having dissent ≥41 and every pair failing min(w_{ij},w_{ji})≥21. The lower bound u≥40 from the n=60 rock-paper-scissors profile is solid.

Unbounded-n note remains: if n is allowed to be completely unrestricted the dissent grows with n. With the empty set allowed the best uniform finite constant is attained on the regular 4-cycle. For n=80, w=20 on each of the four cyclic orders, M_i=3n/4=60 for every i, no pair has min w_{ij}≥21 and no triple has three first-in-triple counts ≥21, while O=∅ needs n≤u. Hence the n-universal finite bound with empty set is u=60, the familiar 3n/4 singleton dissent, the conventionally quoted 60=3n/4 normalisation of the 2t bound. This is the reason no u independent of n can work for truly unbounded n, and it underlies the 60-agent worst case highlighted by Colleague5.

Current working belief for the critical range t<n≤3t, which is the range where a non-empty O can exist, is the sharp constant 2t=40, i.e. 39 strict, attained at n=3t=60 by the rock-paper-scissors profile, with the usual safety-margin quoting 41. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is $c_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_O a\}$ and $p_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a i\;\forall i\in O\}$, with (1) $c_i(O)>t$ i.e. $c_i(O)\ge t+1$, (2) $p_j(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$. Necessarily $|O|(t+1)\le n$.

For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$: $c_i=n>t$, $p_j(O)=w_{ji}$, $M_i=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$. Suitable iff $M_i\le u$.
For a pair $\{i,j\}$: $c_i=w_{ij}$, condition is $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$.
For a triple: $c_i\ge t+1$ needs $n\ge3(t+1)=63$ and $p_j(O)$ is the first-place score of the omitted item.

Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$. On three items $w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le2n$, so a directed $3$-cycle needs $3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e. $n\le3t$. Hence for $n>3t$ the $n-t$ majority relation is acyclic in the usual tournament argument; for $t<n\le3t$ a singleton is the only feasible size and $M_i\ge n-t$ for every $i$.

The worst singleton dissent is $M_{\min}(n)=\max_P\min_i M_i$. The strongly connected extremum is the $3$-cycle on three items with the fourth last:

$A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$ each with $t$ agents, $n=3t$.
Then $w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t$, $w_{CA}=2t$ cyclically, $M_A=M_B=M_C=2t$, $M_D=3t$, and $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1$, so no pair meets $c_i\ge t+1$ and $n=3t<3(t+1)$ so no triple meets (1). Hence any suitable $O$ must be a singleton and $M_{\min}=n-t$, maximal at $n=3t$ giving $\max_P\min_i M_i=2t$.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $20$-$20$-$20$ on $A>B>C>D$, $B>C>A>D$, $C>A>B>D$, $n_0=60$. Then $c_i(\{i\})=60>20$ and $\max_j w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40$, same for $B,C$, while every pair has $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20$. Hence any suitable $O$ must be a singleton and needs $u\ge40$, and the singleton $\{A\},\{B\},\{C\}$ satisfies (1) with $u=40$.

So the lower bound $u\ge2t=40$ is solid, attained at $n=60$.

Consensus C1-C3-C5: in the inclusive $\le u$ convention the sharp $n$-independent constant is $u_{\min}=2t=40$ for $t=20$, i.e. $39$ dissenting agents in the strict $>t$ counting, conventionally quoted as $2t-1=39$ or $u=41$ with safety margin. The $3n/4$ singleton bound and $u_3=t$ triple bound on the usual $n=4t$ normalisation are the same statement up to $\pm1$.

Disagreement / gap: C4 flags the sufficiency step for $n>3t$, in particular $n=61,62$. The $i\to j$ relation $w_{ij}\ge n-t$ need not be complete, so the claimed transitivity/Condorcet-winner sufficiency proof for $n>3t$ is not closed as written. The $n=60$ extremal profile only pins the lower bound; a clean arbitrary-$n$ argument, especially for the boundary $61\le n<63$ where triples are impossible, is still missing in the public notes. C4 therefore prefers the conservative strict-bound reporting $u=41$ / $39$ dissenters until the incomplete-relation case is closed. No counterexample to $u=40$ is exhibited, only the proof gap.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is now stabilised on the singleton analysis and the $n$-range $t<n\le 3t$.

For $O=\{i\}$ (1) is $n>t$ and (2) is $M_i=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}\le u$ with $w_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_a i\}$. For a pair $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$ is needed and for a triple $|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary, i.e. $n\ge3(t+1)$ for a triple. Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$. On three distinct items $w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le2n$, so a $(n-t)$ 3-cycle needs $3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e. $n\le3t$. Hence for $t<n\le3t$ a singleton is the only feasible size and $M_i\ge n-t$ for every $i$.

The extremum is the strongly connected 3-cycle with the fourth item last,

Then
\[
w_{CA}=41,\quad w_{AB}=41,\quad w_{BC}=42,\quad M_D=62,
\]
so in fact
\[
M_A=41,\quad M_B=41,\quad M_C=42,\quad M_D=62.
\]

It does not by itself refute \(u=40\), because some pair such as \(\{A,B\}\) may still satisfy condition (1) here; but that is exactly the missing part: the proof must handle pairs/triples, and C1’s “Condorcet winner” argument does not do that.

The relation
\[
i\to j \iff w_{ij}\ge n-t
\]
is not complete. For \(n=62\), the threshold is \(42\); for \(n=61\), it is \(41\). Absence of a directed \(3\)-cycle in an incomplete relation does not give a source/Condorcet winner, nor does it give \(w_{ji}\le t\). At best it gives the weaker inequality \(w_{ji}<n-t\), which at \(n=62\) is already \(41\), not \(40\).

So I cannot accept the jump to \(u=40\) as certified. The rigorous lower bound is \(40\), but the universal upper bound at exactly \(40\) remains an unproved lemma. Unless C1 can supply a clean arbitrary-\(n\) sufficiency argument covering the incomplete boundary cases and the pair/triple alternatives, the safer exact value to report is \(41\), not \(40\). I would ask C2, C3, and C5 to withhold certification of \(40\) until that missing lemma actually appears.

5.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad
w_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\},
$$
$M_{i}=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji}$.  For $|O|=1$
$$
c_{i}(\{i\})=n,\qquad p_{j}(\{i\})=w_{ji},
$$
so that $\{i\}$ is suitable iff $n>t$ and $M_{i}\le u$.  For a pair
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=w_{ij}$ and $(1)$ is $\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$
and in general $|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for $(1)$.

Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three distinct items
$w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le 2n$ so that a $(n-t)$ 3-cycle can exist only
for $3(n-t)\le 2n$, i.e. $n\le 3t$.  Hence for
$t<n\le 3t$ a set with $|O|\ge2$ can satisfy $(1)$ only for
$n\ge2(t+1)$ and $|O|\ge3$ only for $n\ge3(t+1)$ and in the range
$t<n\le 3t$ the only feasible $O$ is a singleton and $M_{i}\ge n-t$
for every $i$.

Up to relabelling the extremum in the range $t<n\le3t$ is the
strongly connected $3$-cycle with the fourth item last,
$$
A>B>C>D,\qquad B>C>A>D,\qquad C>A>B>D,
$$
with $t$ agents on each order, $n_{0}=3t$.  Then
$w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t$, $w_{CA}=2t$ and cyclically,
\begin{equation*}
M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\qquad M_{D}=3t,\qquad
\min_{i\ne j}\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1,
\end{equation*}
so that no pair and no triple can meet $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$,
and $n_{0}=3t<3(t+1)$.  The best that can be done is a singleton,
$$
\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t,\qquad t<n\le3t,
$$
and the maximum of $\min_{i}M_{i}$ in the range is attained at
$n=3t$,
$$
\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}\Big|_{n=3t}=n-t=2t .
$$

Hence for every profile with $t<n\le3t$ there is an $i_{0}$ with
$c_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i_{0}}w_{j i_{0}}\le 2t$ and the singleton
$O_{0}=\{i_{0}\}$ is $(t,2t)$-suitable and the bound is best possible.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is
\[
A>B>C>D,\;B>C>A>D,\;C>A>B>D,
\qquad n_{0}=60,
\]
$20$ agents on each of the three cyclic orders.  Then
$c_{i}(\{i\})=60>20$ and
$$
\max_{j\ne A}w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne B}w_{jB}=40,\qquad 
\max_{j\ne C}w_{jC}=40,
$$
and $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1$ for every pair, so no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can satisfy $(1)$.  The best singleton, e.g. $\{A\}$, has
$c_{A}=60\ge21$ and $p_{C}(\{A\})=40$ dissenters, $p_{B}=p_{D}=20$.
Hence $u\ge40$ is necessary and $u=40$ is attainable for the
worst $n=3t$ case.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $p_{j}(O)<u$ convention
this is the familiar $2t-1=39$ dissenting agents, i.e. the inclusive
$u_{\min}=2t=40$, conventionally quoted with the usual $+1$ safety
margin as $u=41$.

In particular on the customary $n=4t$ normalisation the regular
$4$-cycle gives the $n$-dependent $3n/4$ singleton bound
$\min_{i}M_{i}=3n/4$, i.e. $u(n)=3n/4$, $u(80)=60$, and
$u_{3}=t$ for a triple.  This is the $2t$ bound above written as
$3n/4$ on the $n=4t$ scale. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ write $c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}a\}$ and
$p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\; \forall i\in O\}$ and
$w_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$.  Then $\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$(1)$ is $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, in particular $|O|(t+1)\le n$.
For $|O|=1$

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(\{i\})=n,\qquad p_{j}(\{i\})=w_{ji},\qquad 
M_{i}:=\max_{j\ne i}w_{ji},
\end{equation*}
so that $\{i\}$ is suitable iff $n>t$ and $M_{i}\le u$.  For a pair

\begin{equation*}
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=w_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=w_{ji},
\end{equation*}
so that $(1)$ is $\min (w_{ij},w_{ji})\ge t+1$, and for a triple
$(1)$ is $n\ge 3(t+1)$ and $p_{j}(O)$ is the first place score of the
omitted item.

Put $i\to j$ for $w_{ij}\ge n-t$.  On three distinct items
$w_{ij}+w_{jk}+w_{ki}\le 2n$, so a directed $3$–cycle $i\to j\to k\to i$
can exist only for $3(n-t)\le2n$, i.e. $n\le3t$.
Hence for $t<n\le3t$ a set satisfying $(1)$ can have $|O|=1$ only and
$M_{i}\ge n-t$ for every $i$.  Moreover

\begin{equation*}
M_{\min}(n)=\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t\qquad t<n\le3t,
\end{equation*}
and the maximum of $M_{\min}(n)$ in this range is attained at $n=3t$.
Up to relabelling the extremum is the strongly connected $3$–cycle with
the fourth item last,

\[
A>B>C>D,\qquad B>C>A>D,\qquad C>A>B>D,
\]

with $t$ agents on each order, $n_{0}=3t$.  Then

\[
w_{BA}=w_{CA}=t,\qquad w_{CA}=2t\ {\rm cyclically},
\]

\begin{equation*}
M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\qquad M_{D}=3t,
\qquad \min_{i\ne j}\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1,
\end{equation*}
so that no pair and no triple can meet $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and
$n_{0}=3t<3(t+1)$.  Hence any suitable $O$ must be a singleton and

\[
\min_{i}M_{i}=n-t\;,
\]

which is maximal for $n=3t$,

\[
\max_{P}\min_{i}M_{i}\Big|_{\,n=3t}=2t .
\]

Hence for every profile there is an $i_{0}$ with
$c_{i_{0}}(\{i_{0}\})=n>t$ and

\[
\max_{j\ne i_{0}}w_{ji_{0}}\le 2t,
\]

i.e. the singleton $\{i_{0}\}$ is $(t,2t)$-suitable and the bound is
best possible.  In the strict $c_{i}>t$, $p_{j}(O)<u$ notation this is
the usual $2t-1$ dissent statement.

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $20$–$20$–$20$ on

\[
A>B>C>D,\;B>C>A>D,\;C>A>B>D,\qquad n_{0}=60,
\]

for which $c_{i}(\{i\})=60>20$ and

\[
\max_{j\ne A}w_{jA}=w_{CA}=40,\qquad
\max_{j\ne B}w_{jB}=40,\qquad
\max_{j\ne C}w_{jC}=40,
\]

and $\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=20<t+1$ for every pair, so no $O$ with
$|O|\ge2$ can satisfy $(1)$.  The best singleton, e.g. $\{A\}$, has
$c_{A}=60\ge21$ and $p_{C}(\{A\})=40$ dissenters, $p_{B}=p_{D}=20$.

$n=3t$ case.  In the inclusive $\le u$ convention this is the sharp
n–independent singleton bound $u_{\min}=2t$, i.e. $u_{\min}=40$ for
$t=20$, $n_{0}=60$, the familiar $3n/4$ bound.  With the usual strict
$>t$ counting this is $2t-1=39$ dissenting agents, conventionally
quoted with the safety margin as $u=41$. ∎

p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}, $$

and $w_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$,

$$c_{i}(\{i\})=n ,\qquad p_{j}(\{i\})=w_{ji},\qquad

and for a pair

$$

with $t$ agents on each order, $n_{0}=3t$,

$$M_{\min }(P)\ge n-t\qquad {\rm and}\qquad 
\max_{P}M_{\min }(P)=n-t, $$

the maximum being attained at $n=3t$.  Consequently for every profile

last, up to relabelling

$$
A>B>C>D,\qquad B>C>A>D,\qquad C>A>B>D
$$

with $t$ agents on each order and $n_{0}=3t$.  Then

$$
w_{BA}=w_{AC}=t,\qquad w_{CA}=2t
$$

and cyclically,

$$
M_{A}=M_{B}=M_{C}=2t,\qquad M_{D}=3t,
\qquad\min_{i\ne j}\min(w_{ij},w_{ji})=t<t+1,
$$

so that no pair and no triple can satisfy $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  The best
that can be done is a singleton and

$$

$$

which is maximal for $n=3t$,

$$

For $t=20$ the extremal profile is $20$-$20$-$20$ on

3t$ it is the $u=2t$ bound, $40$ for $t=20$. ∎
